q.q: The branch that studies insects is:
q.explanation: Entomology = insects; herpeto = reptiles/amphibians, ornitho = birds, ichthyo = fish.

q.q: Physiology differs from anatomy because it studies:
q.explanation: Anatomy = what parts are; physiology = what parts DO.

q.q: The study of living things at the level of DNA and proteins is ____ biology.
q.answer: molecular
q.explanation: Molecular biology — life's chemistry machinery.

q.q: Why does fighting malaria need MORE than one biology branch?
q.answer: parasite mosquito human spread|multiple levels|entomology parasitology epidemiology
q.explanation: Plasmodium (parasitology), Anopheles vector (entomology), human response (immunology/physiology), population spread (epidemiology/ecology).

q.q: Microbiology and bacteriology mean exactly the same thing.
q.explanation: Bacteriology is only bacteria; microbiology covers bacteria, viruses, fungi, protists.

q.q: A scientist studies how Lake Tana fish interact with their environment. Her main branch is:
q.explanation: Organisms ↔ environment = ecology (freshwater/limnology flavour).

q.q: Pick the correct organisation ladder (small → large):
options: Cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism
q.explanation: The standard hierarchy from cell upward.

q.q: The computational analysis of DNA sequence data is called ____.
q.answer: bioinformatics
q.explanation: Biology + informatics — the data-driven branch.

q.q: Give the branch and level for: 'studying how a hormone lowers blood sugar'.
q.answer: physiology endocrine|organ system level|function of hormone
q.explanation: Physiology (function), specifically endocrine physiology, at organ-system level.

q.q: Basic (pure) research is best described as research aimed at:
q.explanation: Knowledge for its own sake — understanding is the goal.

q.q: Which is an APPLIED biology example?
q.explanation: Barley breeding solves a farmer's problem — applied.

q.q: The heat-stable DNA polymerase used in PCR came from the bacterium Thermus ____.
q.answer: aquaticus|taq
q.explanation: T. aquaticus from hot springs — the pure-research gift to diagnostics.

q.q: Why can cutting pure-research funding hurt a country's medicine 20 years later?
q.answer: no new discoveries|pipeline dries|applications need basic science
q.explanation: Applications draw on basic discoveries; without new curiosity research, tomorrow's tools must be imported at premium cost.

q.q: Biotechnology only means modern genetic engineering.
q.explanation: Bread, beer, injera fermentation are biotechnology too — using organisms to make products.

q.q: The discovery chain in correct order is:
q.explanation: Question first, then understanding, then usable tool, then product.

q.q: Ethiopia's public-health laboratory and outbreak-response institution is abbreviated ____.
q.answer: ephi
q.explanation: Ethiopian Public Health Institute — applied biology in action.

q.q: Classify: 'studying how cichlid fish species diversified in lakes' and 'using that knowledge to manage a fishery'.
q.answer: pure applied|first basic second applied|understanding vs management
q.explanation: Evolutionary curiosity = pure; sustainable fishery = applied.

q.q: CRISPR gene editing originated from:
q.explanation: Bacterial anti-viral defence observed as basic science → the editing tool (2012).

q.q: Cell theory states all of the following EXCEPT:
options: All organisms are made of cells
The cell is the basic unit of life
Cells can form from sterile broth
q.explanation: Spontaneous generation was disproved (Pasteur); cells only come from cells.

q.q: The 1859 book 'On the Origin of Species' was written by ____.
q.answer: darwin|charles darwin
q.explanation: Charles Darwin — with Wallace's parallel work read out in 1858.

q.q: Mendel's inheritance units are now called:
q.explanation: His 'factors' = genes, on chromosomes (established ~1900-1902).

q.q: What did Pasteur's swan-neck flasks prove?
q.answer: life from life|microbes from air particles|no spontaneous generation
q.explanation: Sterile broth stayed sterile until particles entered — biogenesis, not spontaneous generation.

q.q: DNA's structure immediately suggested its function because:
options: Base pairing allows each strand to template a new one
q.explanation: Complementarity (A-T, G-C) = a built-in copying mechanism.

q.q: Pick the correct chronological order:
options: DNA helix → germ theory → cell theory
Cell theory → germ theory → DNA helix
Germ theory → DNA helix → cell theory
DNA helix → cell theory → germ theory
q.explanation: 1838 cells → 1860s-80s germs → 1953 DNA.

q.q: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray diffraction data was essential to the DNA model.
q.explanation: Photo 51 gave the helix dimensions; her contribution is now recognised.

q.q: The rules linking a specific microbe to a specific disease are ____'s postulates.
q.answer: koch
q.explanation: Robert Koch (1884) — the causation checklist still used conceptually.

q.q: How does the discovery of natural selection explain antibiotic resistance?
q.answer: resistant variants selected|survive and reproduce|pre-existing variation
q.explanation: Variation exists; antibiotics kill susceptible bacteria; resistant survivors multiply — selection in fast-forward.

q.q: The only human disease eradicated so far is:
q.explanation: Smallpox — certified eradicated 1980 through vaccination.

q.q: The first recombinant-DNA human drug (1982) was ____.
q.answer: insulin
q.explanation: Bacteria engineered to make human insulin — diabetes treatment transformed.

q.q: Why did clean water save more lives than hospitals?
q.answer: prevention at population scale|stops transmission|germ theory public health
q.explanation: Water/sanitation cut infectious transmission for everyone, not just those who could reach a hospital.

q.q: The Green Revolution mainly doubled yields of:
q.explanation: High-yielding dwarf wheat and rice varieties — staple calories.

q.q: Antibiotics cause bacteria to mutate into resistant forms.
q.explanation: Resistance arises by random mutation FIRST; antibiotics select the resistant ones (natural selection).

q.q: DNA-based identity testing for forensics was developed by Alec ____ in 1984.
q.answer: jeffreys
q.explanation: Sir Alec Jeffreys — genetic fingerprinting.

q.q: Which technology lets a single banana plant produce thousands of disease-free plantlets?
q.explanation: Micropropagation from meristem culture — cell biology's farm gift (used at EBI, Ethiopia).

q.q: Name the discovery behind each: (a) safe surgery in 1870, (b) drought-tolerant teff variety, (c) catching a criminal from blood at a scene.
q.answer: germ theory|genetics breeding|dna profiling
q.explanation: (a) germ theory → antisepsis (Lister); (b) Mendel/evolution → breeding; (c) DNA structure → profiling.

q.q: Pick the correct sequence of contributions:
q.explanation: Public health (1850s-70s) → antisepsis (1867) → antibiotics (1940s) → biotech drug (1982).

q.q: The Omo I fossils are significant because they are among the oldest:
q.explanation: ~195,000 (restudied ~233,000) years — early modern humans, Ethiopian Rift.

q.q: The Ethiopian paleoanthropologist who co-described Herto is Berhane ____.
q.answer: asfaw
q.explanation: Berhane Asfaw — AAU professor, National Museum leader.

q.q: 'Lucy' (Dinkinesh) belongs to the species:
q.explanation: 3.2 Ma A. afarensis — a distant relative on the human family tree.

q.q: Why is the 2017 teff genome an applied contribution, not just data?
q.answer: breeding markers|yield drought lodging|precision breeding
q.explanation: It pinpoints genes so breeders select sturdy, high-yield teff fast — food security tool.

q.q: Enset is a variety of banana.
q.explanation: 'False banana' — different genus; a uniquely Ethiopian staple crop.

q.q: The world's rarest canid, endemic to Ethiopian highlands, is the Ethiopian ____.
q.answer: wolf
q.explanation: Canis simensis — ~500 left, Bale Mountains.

q.q: Arabica coffee's wild origin is in:
q.explanation: SW Ethiopian highlands — the gene pool the world's coffee descends from.

q.q: How does highland-living research show natural selection acting on humans?
q.answer: adaptation oxygen hemoglobin|genetic physiological|altitude
q.explanation: Highlanders show distinct oxygen/hemoglobin handling — population-level adaptation to low oxygen.

q.q: Pick the correct fossil-age order (oldest first):
q.explanation: Lucy 3.2 Ma (oldest) → Omo I ~230 ka → Herto ~160 ka.

q.q: Which tissue is responsible for a plant growing TALLER?
q.explanation: Apical meristems at shoot/root tips add length (primary growth).

q.q: All of these are living tissues EXCEPT:
q.explanation: Functional xylem is dead — hollow pipes. The others are living cells.

q.q: The waxy layer on leaf surfaces that limits water loss is the ____.
q.answer: cuticle
q.explanation: Cuticle = epicuticular wax over epidermis.

q.q: Why are sclerenchyma fibres useful to humans, and give one fibre crop?
q.answer: strong threads textile|flax linen|jute hemp
q.explanation: Long dead lignified cells = natural high-strength threads — flax→linen, jute, hemp.

q.q: Girdling kills a tree because it removes:
q.explanation: Bark = phloem; roots starve of leaf sugar while water still rises through wood.

q.q: Guard cells contain chloroplasts and change shape to open/close stomata.
q.explanation: They photosynthesise, pump ions, swell (open) or shrink (close).

q.q: Annual tree rings are layers of which tissue?
q.answer: xylem|secondary xylem|wood
q.explanation: Cambium adds a xylem ring each season.

q.q: Explain why 'dead' xylem is actually BETTER for water transport.
q.answer: hollow no cytoplasm|lignin resists collapse|open pipes
q.explanation: Dead cells leave hollow, lignin-reinforced tubes — no cytoplasm blocking flow, walls resist tension collapse.

q.q: Pick the correct tissue→function pairing order (protection, packing, flexible support, rigidity):
q.explanation: Skin → packing/storage → bendy props → dead armour.

q.q: The deep, single dominant root system of dicots is called:
q.explanation: Taproot: one main root with side branches (carrot, bean).

q.q: Most photosynthesis in a leaf happens in the:
q.explanation: Palisade cells pack the most chloroplasts, just under the transparent top.

q.q: After fertilisation, the ovary of a flower develops into the ____.
q.answer: fruit
q.explanation: Ovary → fruit; ovules → seeds.

q.q: Prove a potato is a stem, not a root.
q.answer: eyes are buds|nodes|sprouts from buds
q.explanation: Potato 'eyes' are buds at nodes — only stems have buds; roots never do.

q.q: Root hairs increase absorption mainly by:
q.explanation: Single-cell extensions multiply epidermal surface ~10×.

q.q: Monocot stems have vascular bundles arranged in a ring with cambium between.
q.explanation: That's dicots; monocots scatter their bundles and lack cambium (no tree rings).

q.q: The male part of a flower (filament + anther) is the ____.
q.answer: stamen
q.explanation: Stamen = pollen factory; female = carpel/pistil.

q.q: Why do cacti have spines instead of broad leaves?
q.answer: reduce water loss|surface area|desert adaptation
q.explanation: Broad leaves transpire hugely; spines = minimal surface + defence; the stem takes over photosynthesis.

q.q: Pick the correct flower structure order (outside → inside):
q.explanation: Sepals protect, petals advertise, stamens ring the central carpel.

q.q: The selective barrier forcing water through cell membranes in roots is the:
q.explanation: Suberin strip in endodermis blocks cell-wall bypass — root controls what enters xylem.

q.q: The raw materials of photosynthesis are:
q.explanation: Carbon dioxide + water, driven by light → sugar + oxygen.

q.q: The green pigment that absorbs light energy is ____.
q.answer: chlorophyll
q.explanation: Chlorophyll a — in thylakoid membranes.

q.q: The O₂ released in photosynthesis comes from:
q.explanation: Photolysis of water — proven with ¹⁸O isotope experiments.

q.q: The Calvin cycle takes place in the:
q.explanation: Stroma fluid holds the fixation enzymes.

q.q: A plant gets plenty of light and water but grows poorly in a sealed, cooled box. Name the likely limiting factor and why.
q.answer: co2 low|carbon dioxide limited|temperature too low enzyme
q.explanation: Sealed = CO₂ runs out; cold = enzyme rates drop — either caps the rate despite light.

q.q: Dark reactions occur only at night.
q.explanation: They run by day using ATP/NADPH from light reactions; they just don't use photons directly.

q.q: How many CO₂ molecules must enter the Calvin cycle to export ONE G3P (3-carbon sugar)?
q.explanation: Each CO₂ adds 1 carbon; 3 turns per G3P exported.

q.q: The enzyme that fixes CO₂ onto RuBP is abbreviated ____.
q.answer: rubisco
q.explanation: Ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase — Earth's most abundant protein.

q.q: Which is NOT a product of the light-dependent reactions?
q.explanation: Glucose (G3P) comes from the Calvin cycle, not the light stage.

q.q: Pick the correct Calvin-cycle order:
q.explanation: CO₂ fixed to RuBP → reduced by ATP/NADPH → RuBP regenerated.

q.q: The main force pulling water up a tall tree is:
q.explanation: Evaporation at leaves creates tension on the cohesive water column.

q.q: Water molecules sticking to each other is called ____.
q.answer: cohesion
q.explanation: Cohesion (H-bonds) keeps the xylem column unbroken.

q.q: Phloem sap moves:
q.explanation: Pressure-flow follows loading/unloading sites — seasonal direction changes.

q.q: Why do stomata close during drought even though it starves the leaf of CO₂?
q.answer: save water priority|turgor loss|ABA closes
q.explanation: Water loss would kill faster than CO₂ shortage; guard cells lose turgor (ABA signal) and seal the pores.

q.q: Guttation droplets are the same as morning dew.
q.explanation: Guttation = xylem sap pushed by root pressure (mineral water from inside); dew = condensed air.

q.q: The Casparian strip forces water/minerals to cross cell membranes in the:
q.explanation: Suberin band blocks the apoplast route — selective control point.

q.q: Yellowing of OLD leaves with green veins suggests a deficiency of which mobile element (symbol)?
q.answer: mg|magnesium
q.explanation: Mg is chlorophyll's centre and phloem-mobile — old leaves are cannibalised first; interveinal pattern.

q.q: How does an aphid stylet experiment support the pressure-flow theory?
q.answer: sap spurts under pressure|positive pressure|osmotic loading
q.explanation: Sap keeps flowing from the severed stylet — phloem is under positive hydrostatic pressure from source osmotic loading.

q.q: Pick the correct water pathway:
options: Root hair → cortex → endodermis → xylem → leaf
q.explanation: Soil → hair → cortex → endodermis gate → xylem highway → leaf.

q.q: Water molecules attract each other because water is:
q.explanation: The dipole (δ⁺H, δ⁻O) enables hydrogen bonding between molecules.

q.q: The weak attraction between water's δ⁺H and a neighbour's δ⁻O is a ____ bond.
q.answer: hydrogen|h-bond
q.explanation: Hydrogen bonds — individually weak, collectively powerful.

q.q: Ice floats because:
options: H-bonds form an open lattice making it less dense
q.explanation: The crystalline lattice spaces molecules apart — solid water is ~9% less dense.

q.q: How does sweating cool the body — name the property involved.
q.answer: latent heat evaporation|evaporation removes heat|high heat of vaporisation
q.explanation: Evaporating sweat absorbs ~2.4 kJ/g of body heat — water's high latent heat.

q.q: Water dissolves oils well because both are liquids.
q.explanation: Like dissolves like: polar water excludes non-polar oils.

q.q: ORS works because glucose drives absorption of ____ ions (name/symbol).
q.answer: sodium|na|na+
q.explanation: Na⁺-glucose co-transport pulls salt, and water follows osmotically.

q.q: Why does a lake freeze from the TOP down instead of the bottom?
q.answer: ice floats insulates|4 degrees densest|cold water on top
q.explanation: Ice is less dense → stays on top; below, water sinks to 4 °C (densest) — the surface freezes first.

q.q: The reaction that BREAKS polymers by adding water is:
q.explanation: Hydrolysis = water splits bonds; condensation joins them losing water.

q.q: Evaporating sweat removes ~2.4 kJ per gram. How many kJ does 50 g of sweat removal cool? (kJ)
q.explanation: 50 × 2.4 = 120 kJ — a workout's heat dumped.

q.q: The ion at the centre of chlorophyll is:
q.explanation: Mg²⁺ sits in chlorophyll's ring — without it, no green.

q.q: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump moves 3 sodium ions ____ and 2 potassium ions ____ per ATP.
q.answer: out;in|out in
q.explanation: 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in — builds the resting potential.

q.q: A goitre (swollen thyroid) indicates deficiency of:
q.explanation: I⁻ is needed for thyroxine; the gland enlarges trying to catch any iodine.

q.q: Why does iron deficiency cause fatigue?
q.answer: less hemoglobin oxygen|anemia|O2 transport drops
q.explanation: Fe²⁺ carries O₂ in haemoglobin; less iron → less oxygen to mitochondria → less ATP → fatigue.

q.q: Nerve impulses travel as electrons moving through the axon like a copper wire.
q.explanation: They are ion waves (Na⁺/K⁺ fluxes across membrane), not electron flow.

q.q: Plant nitrate deficiency first shows as:
q.explanation: N is mobile — pulled from old leaves to new growth → general old-leaf yellowing + stunting.

q.q: The phosphate-containing energy currency of cells is ____.
q.answer: atp
q.explanation: ATP — adenosine triphosphate; its bonds power cellular work.

q.q: Explain why severe diarrhoea can kill a child even if they drink plenty of plain water.
q.answer: electrolyte loss|dilution|ion balance fails
q.explanation: Diarrhoea drains Na⁺/K⁺/HCO₃⁻; plain water dilutes what remains → nerve/heart function and pH collapse — ORS (salt+glucose) is the fix.

q.q: Calcium's roles include all EXCEPT:
q.explanation: O₂ transport is iron's job (haemoglobin); Ca²⁺ does clotting, contraction, bone.

q.q: The monomer of proteins is the:
q.explanation: 20 amino acids → peptide bonds → polypeptides.

q.q: Iodine solution turning blue-black proves the presence of:
q.explanation: Iodine slips into starch's helix → blue-black.

q.q: The bond linking two amino acids is a ____ bond.
q.answer: peptide
q.explanation: Peptide bond (condensation, −H₂O).

q.q: Why do humans get no energy from cellulose even though it is made of glucose?
q.answer: beta bonds|no cellulase|fibre
q.explanation: Our enzymes can't hydrolyse β-glycosidic bonds — only microbes (ruminants, our gut partly) can.

q.q: Which lipid property makes it the best long-term energy store?
q.explanation: Double the energy per gram of carbs, without water weight.

q.q: Enzymes are consumed in the reactions they catalyse.
q.explanation: Catalysts emerge unchanged — one enzyme molecule works thousands of times.

q.q: The test reagent that turns violet with proteins is ____.
q.answer: biuret
q.explanation: Biuret reagent (alkaline CuSO₄) + peptide bonds → violet.

q.q: DNA's building blocks are:
q.explanation: Nucleotides: sugar + phosphate + base (A/T/G/C).

q.q: A fever 'cooks' an enzyme. Use structure terms to explain what stops working.
q.answer: tertiary unfolds|active site shape|denature
q.explanation: Heat breaks weak bonds holding tertiary structure → active site distorts → substrate no longer fits.

q.q: Pick the correct protein structure hierarchy:
q.explanation: Sequence → local folds → 3D → multi-chain assembly.

q.q: DNA replication occurs during:
q.explanation: S = Synthesis — the only phase where DNA is copied.

q.q: The 'resting' label for interphase is wrong because interphase is when the cell:
q.explanation: It's the busiest phase — growth + replication + checks.

q.q: The tumour-suppressor protein nicknamed 'guardian of the genome' is ____.
q.explanation: p53 halts damaged cells at G1 for repair or apoptosis.

q.q: Why do cells STOP growing and divide instead of getting bigger and bigger?
q.answer: surface volume diffusion|too big starves|SA:V limit
q.explanation: Volume grows faster than surface — big cells can't exchange enough material; division restores a workable SA:V.

q.q: Neurons normally remain in G0 and do not divide.
q.explanation: Most mature neurons are post-mitotic — brain injury damage is largely permanent.

q.q: The M (spindle) checkpoint ensures:
options: All chromosomes attach to spindle before anaphase
q.explanation: It blocks anaphase until every kinetochore is attached — prevents wrong chromosome numbers.

q.q: Cycle = 20 h; 5% of cells are in M phase. Approximate M duration in hours?
Programmed, clean cell death is called ____.
q.answer: apoptosis
q.explanation: The safety option when damage is beyond repair.

q.q: Pick the correct phase order:
q.explanation: G1 grow → S copy → G2 check → M divide.

q.q: Explain why a p53 mutation so often leads to cancer.
q.answer: no brake|damaged DNA replicated|checkpoint fails
q.explanation: Without p53, damaged cells skip the G1 halt, replicate mutations, and accumulate the driver changes of cancer.

q.q: The correct mitosis order is:
q.explanation: PMAT — the mnemonic that never fails.

q.q: Sister chromatids separate during:
q.explanation: Anaphase: cohesin cut, chromatids pulled poleward.

q.q: The structure where two sister chromatids join is the ____.
q.answer: centromere
q.explanation: The centromere — the 'handshake' point.

q.q: Why is metaphase the best stage to photograph chromosomes for a karyotype?
q.answer: most condensed|lined up equator|easy count
q.explanation: Maximum condensation + single-file alignment = clear, countable chromosomes.

q.q: Plant cells complete cytokinesis by building a:
q.explanation: Vesicles fuse into a cell plate that becomes the new wall.

q.q: A dog cell (2n = 78) completes mitosis. Chromosomes per daughter cell?
q.explanation: Mitosis preserves number: 78 → 78 + 78.

q.q: The nuclear envelope dissolves during prophase/prometaphase.
q.explanation: It must break down for spindle fibres to reach chromosomes.

q.q: How does mitosis explain why a rose cutting flowers exactly like the parent?
q.answer: identical copies|same genes|clone
q.explanation: Mitotic daughters inherit the parent's identical genome — the cutting is a genetic clone.

q.q: Pick the correct chromatid/chromosome count story for a human cell:
options: G2: 46 chr, 92 chromatids → anaphase: 92 chr → daughters: 46 each
q.explanation: Replication doubles chromatids; separation doubles countable chromosomes briefly; cytokinesis restores 46.

q.q: Crossing over occurs during:
q.explanation: Prophase I — paired homologues swap segments at chiasmata.

q.q: The chromosome-number reduction (2n → n) happens in:
q.explanation: MI separates homologues — the reductional division.

q.q: A human sperm contains ____ chromosomes.
q.explanation: Haploid gamete; 23 + 23 at fertilisation = 46.

q.q: Why does meiosis produce FOUR cells but oogenesis yields only ONE functional egg?
q.answer: polar bodies|cytoplasm for embryo|uneven division
q.explanation: Eggs need cytoplasm/yolk for early development — unequal cytokinesis packs it into one cell; the rest become polar bodies.

q.q: Independent assortment means:
options: Homologue pairs orient randomly at metaphase I
q.explanation: Each pair's maternal/paternal side faces either pole randomly → 2²³ combinations.

q.q: An organism with 2n = 8: how many independent-assortment gamete types (no crossing over)?
q.explanation: n = 4 pairs → 2⁴ = 16.

q.q: DNA replication occurs before both meiosis I and meiosis II.
q.explanation: Only once — before meiosis I; interkinesis has no S phase.

q.q: A child has trisomy 21. Describe the meiotic error that could cause it.
q.answer: nondisjunction|homologues or sisters fail to separate|24-chromosome gamete
q.explanation: Nondisjunction in MI or MII → gamete with two chr-21 (n+1 = 24) + normal gamete (23) = 47, +21.

q.q: Pick the correct meiosis-I sequence:
options: Pairing → crossing over → alignment as pairs → homologue separation
Alignment → pairing → sisters split → crossing over
q.explanation: Prophase I pairing + swap → metaphase I pairs align → anaphase I homologues part.

q.q: Genetic uniqueness of gametes comes from:
options: Crossing over + independent assortment + random fertilisation
q.explanation: Three stacked shuffling events — meiosis is variation engineering.

q.q: Bile helps fat digestion by:
q.explanation: Bile salts increase surface area — lipase does the actual cutting.

q.q: Pepsin works best at pH:
q.explanation: Stomach acid ~pH 2 — pepsin's optimum; it stops in the duodenum's alkaline flow.

q.q: The finger-like absorptive projections of the small intestine are ____.
q.answer: villi|villus
q.explanation: Villi (with microvilli) — the surface-area amplifiers.

q.q: Where do absorbed fatty acids go first, and why not straight to blood?
q.answer: lacteal lymph|too big for capillaries|chylomicrons
q.explanation: Reassembled into chylomicrons — too large for capillaries, so they enter the leaky lacteal (lymph) → bloodstream via thoracic duct.

q.q: Most chemical digestion and absorption happens in the:
q.explanation: Duodenum finishes chemistry; jejunum/ileum absorb — the canal's workhorse.

q.q: The vessel carrying nutrient blood from gut to liver is the ____ portal vein.
q.answer: hepatic
q.explanation: Hepatic portal vein — the liver's first-pass checkpoint.

q.q: Vitamin C must be digested before absorption.
q.explanation: Vitamins are small molecules — absorbed as-is; only polymers need digestion.

q.q: Explain why a high-fibre diet prevents constipation using water and gut facts.
q.answer: fibre holds water|bulk|peristalsis
q.explanation: Cellulose fibre is indigestible but holds water → bulky soft faeces → stimulates peristalsis → regular transit.

q.q: Pick the correct protein-digestion sequence:
options: Pepsin (stomach) → trypsin (duodenum) → peptidases → amino acids absorbed
q.explanation: Stomach starts (peptides), pancreas continues, brush-border finishes to amino acids.

q.q: A villus is 0.5 mm long; microvilli multiply surface ~20×. If the intestine's flat area were 6.5 m², approximate effective area (m²)?
q.explanation: 6.5 × 20 ≈ 130 m² (textbook estimates reach ~200 with folds) — a sports field in your abdomen.

q.q: The chamber pumping oxygenated blood to the body is the:
q.explanation: LV — thickest wall, feeds the aorta and the whole systemic circuit.

q.q: Gas exchange with tissues occurs in:
q.explanation: One-cell-thin walls + slow flow = diffusion happens in capillaries.

q.q: The protein in red cells that carries oxygen is ____.
q.answer: hemoglobin|haemoglobin
q.explanation: Haemoglobin — iron at its centre binds O₂.

q.q: Why does the left ventricle have a much thicker wall than the right?
q.answer: body pressure vs lungs|systemic circuit|pulmonary is low pressure
q.explanation: LV drives blood the whole body against high resistance; RV only pushes to nearby, low-pressure lungs.

q.q: The pulmonary artery is unusual because it carries:
q.explanation: It's an artery by DIRECTION (away from RV) — but the blood is deoxygenated, heading to the lungs.

q.q: The heart's natural pacemaker is the ____ node.
q.answer: sa|sinoatrial
q.explanation: SA node fires the rhythm; AV node delays it so atria empty first.

q.q: Veins contain one-way valves to prevent backflow.
q.explanation: Valves + skeletal-muscle squeeze walk blood uphill to the heart.

q.q: Explain two ways the lymphatic system supports circulation and nutrition.
q.answer: returns leaked fluid|absorbs fat lacteals
q.explanation: (1) Recovers ~3 L/day of leaked plasma → returns it to blood (volume/pressure). (2) Lacteals absorb dietary fats too big for blood capillaries.

q.q: Heart rate 75/min, stroke volume 70 mL. Cardiac output per minute (L)?
q.explanation: 75 × 70 = 5250 mL ≈ 5.25 L/min — the whole blood volume every minute.

q.q: Pick the correct clotting sequence:
options: Fibrin → platelets stick → wound closes → clot
Damage → platelets stick + chemicals → fibrinogen → fibrin mesh → clot
q.explanation: Platelet plug first, then the fibrin net reinforces it into a clot.

q.q: Gas exchange occurs in the:
q.explanation: Alveoli — thin, wet, capillary-wrapped sacs.

q.q: During inspiration, the diaphragm:
q.explanation: Flattening enlarges the cavity → pressure falls → air in.

q.q: Most CO₂ is transported as ____ ions in plasma.
q.answer: bicarbonate|hco3
q.explanation: ~70% as HCO₃⁻ (carbonic anhydrase in RBCs makes it).

q.q: Why does breathing speed up during exercise? Name the signal.
q.answer: CO2 rises pH drops|medulla senses|more O2 demand
q.explanation: Muscles make CO₂/lactic acid → blood pH falls → chemoreceptors → medulla increases rate/depth.

q.q: Surfactant's job is to:
options: Reduce surface tension so alveoli stay open
q.explanation: Without it, small alveoli collapse each breath.

q.q: Exhaled air contains no oxygen.
q.explanation: ~16% O₂ remains — exchange is partial each pass.

q.q: The cilia-and-mucus defence of the trachea is nicknamed the ____ ___.
q.answer: mucociliary escalator
q.explanation: It sweeps trapped particles up to be swallowed.

q.q: Explain one advantage of Ethiopia's highland altitude for endurance athletes.
q.answer: more red cells|EPO|thinner air trains carriers
q.explanation: Lower pO₂ → kidneys release EPO → more RBCs/haemoglobin → greater O₂ carrying capacity when racing at lower altitude.

q.q: Tidal volume 500 mL, rate 14/min. Minute ventilation (L/min)?
q.explanation: 500 × 14 = 7000 mL = 7 L/min at rest.

q.q: The filtering knot of capillaries in a nephron is the:
q.explanation: Glomerulus inside Bowman's capsule — ultrafiltration site.

q.q: Glucose normally disappears from filtrate by:
q.explanation: It IS filtered, then 100% reabsorbed (Na⁺ co-transport) — until the threshold.

q.q: The hormone that increases water reabsorption in the collecting duct is ____.
q.answer: adh|antidiuretic hormone|vasopressin
q.explanation: ADH inserts aquaporins — water returns to blood.

q.q: Why is the renal ARTERY blood dirtier (more urea) than the renal VEIN?
q.answer: kidney removes waste|vein is cleaned|artery brings waste
q.explanation: Artery delivers wastes for filtration; vein carries the cleaned blood away — the kidney is the filter.

q.q: Urea is produced mainly by the:
q.explanation: Liver deaminates excess amino acids → urea → blood → kidney excretes.

q.q: A person with diabetes insipidus has high blood sugar.
q.explanation: It's an ADH problem (water balance) — blood glucose is normal; the name is a trap.

q.q: The functional unit of the kidney is the ____.
q.answer: nephron
q.explanation: ~1 million per kidney.

q.q: Explain how dialysis uses the dialysate recipe to remove urea but keep glucose.
q.answer: no urea in dialysate|diffuses out|same glucose no gradient
q.explanation: Diffusion follows gradients: urea absent outside → leaves blood; glucose matched → no net movement.

q.q: 180 L filtrate/day, 1.5 L urine. What % of filtrate is reabsorbed?
Which is a NON-specific defence?
q.explanation: Phagocytes eat anything foreign — innate, no specificity.

q.q: Antibodies are produced by:
q.explanation: Activated B cells → plasma cells = antibody factories.

q.q: The molecule on a pathogen's surface that triggers an immune response is an ____.
q.answer: antigen
q.explanation: Antigen = the 'non-self' name tag.

q.q: Why does a second infection of the same pathogen often cause no symptoms?
q.answer: memory cells|faster stronger response|secondary
q.explanation: Memory B/T cells mount a 1–3 day high-titre response that clears the pathogen before illness develops.

q.q: HIV primarily destroys:
q.explanation: CD4 helper T — losing the coordinator collapses both antibody and cell-mediated immunity.

q.q: The antibody class behind immediate allergy/anaphylaxis is ____.
q.answer: ige
q.explanation: IgE cross-links on mast cells → histamine flood.

q.q: Vaccines work by giving the body a weakened or partial form of the antigen.
q.explanation: Safe preview → artificial active immunity without the disease.

q.q: Explain how 90% vaccine coverage protects the 10% who aren't vaccinated.
q.answer: herd immunity|pathogen can't spread|breaks chain
q.explanation: With most hosts immune, transmission chains die out — the pathogen rarely reaches unprotected people.

q.q: Pick the correct first-response order after a cut:
options: Vasoconstriction + platelets plug → histamine/inflammation → phagocytes arrive → antibodies (if needed)
q.explanation: Clot first, inflammation signals next, phagocytes patrol, adaptive follows only if antigens appear.

q.q: All the tilapia living in one lake form a:
q.explanation: One species in one area = population.

q.q: In a food chain, the arrows represent:
q.explanation: Grass → zebra: energy moves from grass into zebra.

q.q: Non-living factors like light and temperature are called ____.
q.answer: abiotic
q.explanation: Abiotic = non-living; biotic = living.

q.q: Producers fix 5000 kJ. Energy at the tertiary consumer level (kJ)?
q.explanation: 5000 → 500 → 50 → 5 (three transfers ×0.1).

q.q: Explain the difference between habitat and niche using one example.
q.answer: address vs role|where vs how it lives
q.explanation: Habitat = where it lives (pond); niche = its role (what it eats, when it hunts, where it breeds) — its 'profession'.

q.q: Which organisms close the nutrient cycle?
q.explanation: Decomposers return minerals from dead matter to soil.

q.q: Energy is recycled within an ecosystem just like carbon.
q.explanation: Energy FLOWS one way (sun → heat); only materials cycle.

q.q: Pick the correct trophic order:
q.explanation: Producer → primary → secondary → tertiary → top.

q.q: Why can a pyramid of numbers be inverted but a pyramid of energy cannot?
q.answer: counts snapshot vs flow|thermodynamics always loses
q.explanation: Numbers count individuals (one big tree, many insects); energy obeys the 10% loss rule at every transfer — always shrinking.

q.q: The increasing concentration of toxins up a food web is ____.
q.answer: biomagnification
q.explanation: Biomagnification — top predators get the concentrated dose.

q.q: B=500, D=350, I=40, E=90. Net population change?
The logistic curve levels off because of:
q.explanation: All limits together = resistance reaching K.

q.q: The maximum population an environment can sustain is its ____ capacity.
q.answer: carrying|k
q.explanation: Carrying capacity (K).

q.q: Growth 2%/yr — doubling time by rule of 70? (years)
Which is density-INDEPENDENT?
q.explanation: Fire kills regardless of population size.

q.q: Mark 80, recapture 50 with 10 marked. Estimated N?
What does a narrow-based, urn-shaped age pyramid predict for the next 30 years?
q.answer: shrinking|ageing|deaths exceed births
q.explanation: Few youth entering breeding → population declines and ages (pension/healthcare pressure).

q.q: A population at carrying capacity has zero births and deaths.
q.explanation: Births = deaths (dynamic equilibrium) — individuals still turn over.

q.q: Pick the logistic phase order:
options: Lag → log/exponential → deceleration → plateau at K
q.explanation: Start slow, explode, brake, settle.

q.q: Explain 'overshoot and dieback' with the reindeer example.
q.answer: past K|habitat damaged|crash below K
q.explanation: Population exceeds K, degrades its food base, then crashes — often below the original K because recovery lags.

q.q: Two species with identical niches in one habitat will:
q.explanation: Gause's principle: one wins, the other is eliminated or displaced.

q.q: A harmless fly wearing wasp stripes is:
q.explanation: Batesian = the harmless liar copies the honest warning.

q.q: Bright colour advertising toxicity is called ____.
q.answer: aposematism|warning coloration
q.explanation: Aposematism — 'I'm dangerous, remember me'.

q.q: Why is intraspecific competition usually more intense than interspecific?
q.answer: identical needs|same niche|exact resource overlap
q.explanation: Same species = identical requirements (food, space, mates) — total niche overlap maximizes contest.

q.q: Rhizobium in legume nodules is which interaction type?
q.explanation: +/+: sugars for fixed nitrogen.

q.q: Pick the malaria transmission chain:
options: Infected human → Anopheles mosquito → new human
q.explanation: Anopheles is the vector: parasite develops in mosquito, injects with next bite.

q.q: Parasites almost always kill their hosts quickly.
q.explanation: Quick death ends the parasite's home — successful parasites transmit before causing harm.

q.q: Explain resource partitioning with the warbler example.
q.answer: split niche|different zones/times|coexistence
q.explanation: Similar species feed in different parts of the same tree (top/middle/bottom/needles) — niche division lets competitors coexist.

q.q: Cattle egrets eating insects flushed by grazing cattle is classically:
q.explanation: Bird +, cattle 0 (though real cases blur toward mutualism).

q.q: Reciprocal evolutionary change between interacting species is ____.
q.answer: coevolution|co-evolution
q.explanation: Co-evolution — the Red Queen chase.

q.q: When balancing an equation, you may change:
q.explanation: Only coefficients — subscripts define the substance.

q.q: What coefficient goes before O₂ when balancing C₃H₈ + _O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O?
q.explanation: O on right: 6 + 4 = 10 → 5 O₂.

q.q: The law behind balancing equations is:
q.explanation: Atoms are rearranged, not created/destroyed — mass is conserved.

q.q: In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, how many moles of water form from 2 mol H₂ and 1 mol O₂?
q.explanation: Coefficients ARE mole ratios: 2:1 → 2.

q.q: Writing H₂O₂ while trying to balance a water equation is acceptable.
q.explanation: That's hydrogen peroxide — a different substance. Only coefficients may change.

q.q: State symbol (aq) means:
q.explanation: Aqueous = dissolved in water.

q.q: Balance Fe + Cl₂ → FeCl₃. What is the coefficient of Fe?
q.explanation: 2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃ (Fe 2, Cl 6 both sides).

q.q: Why is the word equation 'magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide' not enough for a scientist?
q.answer: no formulas no amounts|need formulas and balancing|doesn't show ratios or states
q.explanation: It hides the actual substances (formulas), the 2:1:2 ratio, and the states — all needed for calculations.

q.q: Pick the correct balanced equation for burning methane:
q.explanation: C 1, H 4→2H₂O, O 4 left = 4 right ✓.

q.q: Balance: _Na + _Cl₂ → _NaCl. Give the coefficient of NaCl.
q.explanation: 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl.

q.q: 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂ is a:
q.explanation: One reactant breaks into two products (thermal decomposition).

q.q: Which metal displaces copper from CuSO₄ solution?
q.explanation: Zinc sits above copper in the series; Ag and Au sit below.

q.q: How do you test the gas from a metal + acid reaction is hydrogen?
q.answer: squeaky pop|lit splint|pop sound
q.explanation: Bring a lit splint near — hydrogen burns with a characteristic squeaky pop.

q.q: Balance: _Al + 3CuSO₄ → _Al₂(SO₄)₃ + _Cu. What coefficient goes on Al?
q.explanation: 2Al + 3CuSO₄ → Al₂(SO₄)₃ + 3Cu.

q.q: The white precipitate when BaCl₂ meets Na₂SO₄ is:
q.explanation: Barium sulfate is insoluble — the classic sulfate test.

q.q: Copper reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to release hydrogen.
q.explanation: Cu is below hydrogen in the reactivity series — no reaction.

q.q: What colour precipitate is PbI₂?
q.answer: yellow
q.explanation: Lead(II) iodide — the famous 'golden rain' precipitate.

q.q: Limited air supply during fuel burning produces dangerous:
q.explanation: Carbon monoxide — odourless, toxic; incomplete combustion.

q.q: Choose the correct decomposition of calcium carbonate:
q.explanation: Metal carbonates decompose to metal oxide + carbon dioxide (on heating).

q.q: Why is rusting iron in oxygen called combination AND oxidation at once?
q.answer: two substances one product|also reacts with oxygen
q.explanation: 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃: two reactants join (combination) and iron gains oxygen (oxidation — next lesson!).

q.q: Oxidation is best defined as:
q.explanation: OIL — Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons).

q.q: In Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu, zinc is:
q.explanation: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻: loses electrons = oxidised (and is the reducing agent).

q.q: The substance that donates electrons is called the ____ agent.
q.answer: reducing
q.explanation: It reduces the other species while being oxidised itself.

q.q: Oxidation and reduction can occur separately in different beakers with no connection.
q.explanation: Electrons lost must be gained — they're always coupled (even if physically separated by a wire, as in a battery).

q.q: How many electrons does one Cu²⁺ ion gain to become Cu atom?
q.explanation: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu — charge drops by 2.

q.q: Why does the mnemonic say the 'reducing agent' gets oxidised?
q.answer: it gives electrons away|role opposite to what it becomes|it reduces something else
q.explanation: By losing electrons it reduces the other species — the agent is named for what it DOES to others, not what happens to it.

q.q: Rusting is best described as:
q.explanation: Iron is oxidised by oxygen — a slow redox, sped up by salt and water.

q.q: Balance the electrons: Cl₂ + _e⁻ → 2Cl⁻. How many electrons?
q.explanation: Two chloride ions each need one electron: Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻.

q.q: Which reaction shows reduction of the underlined substance? (underlined first)
q.explanation: CuO loses oxygen / Cu²⁺ gains electrons — that's reduction. The others are oxidations.

q.q: Pick the correct half-equation for magnesium acting as a reducing agent:
q.explanation: A reducing agent LOSES electrons: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻.

q.q: How many moles in 36 g of water? (H₂O = 18 g/mol)
How many molecules are in 0.5 mol of CO₂? (answer in units of 10²³, e.g. 3.01)
Molar mass of Ca(OH)₂ in g/mol? (Ca=40, O=16, H=1)
In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, moles of water from 4 mol H₂ (excess O₂)?
q.explanation: Ratio H₂:H₂O = 2:2 = 1:1 → 4 mol.

q.q: Mass of 3 mol of Fe? (Fe = 56 g/mol)
Why is the balanced equation essential before any mole-ratio calculation?
q.answer: ratios come from coefficients|coefficients give mole ratio|must balance first
q.explanation: The coefficients ARE the mole ratios — wrong coefficients, wrong everything downstream.

q.q: Volume of 2 mol CO₂ at STP in litres? (22.4 L/mol)
2 mol A + 5 mol B react as A + 2B → C. The limiting reactant is:
q.explanation: A: 2/1 = 2; B: 5/2 = 2.5 → smaller quotient (A) runs out first.

q.q: Actual yield 9 g, theoretical 15 g. Percentage yield?
Avogadro's constant is approximately 6.022 × 10 to what power?
q.explanation: 6.022×10²³ particles per mole.

q.q: How many ATOMS (in 10²³) are in 1 mol of O₂ molecules?
q.explanation: 1 mol O₂ = 6.022×10²³ molecules × 2 atoms each = 12.044×10²³ atoms.

q.q: Which is a homogeneous mixture?
q.explanation: Uniform throughout at particle level — a true solution.

q.q: A light beam becomes visible passing through it. The sample is a:
q.explanation: Tyndall scattering = colloid (solutions too fine, suspensions settle/filter).

q.q: In salt water, the water is the ____ and the salt is the ____.
q.answer: solute;solvent|solvent solute
q.explanation: Solvent dissolves (water); solute gets dissolved (salt).

q.q: Explain 'like dissolves like' in one sentence with an example.
q.answer: polar dissolves polar|nonpolar in nonpolar|oil petrol
q.explanation: Substances dissolve in solvents with matching intermolecular forces — polar water dissolves salt/sugar; non-polar petrol dissolves oil.

q.q: Stirring increases how much sugar can dissolve in cold water.
q.explanation: Stirring speeds the RATE; the saturation amount (solubility) depends on temperature, not stirring.

q.q: Gas solubility in water usually:
q.explanation: Warm water releases dissolved gases — warm cola goes flat, warm lakes hold less O₂.

q.q: A solution holding more dissolved solute than its saturation point (unstable) is ____.
q.answer: supersaturated
q.explanation: Supersaturated — seed it and it crystallises instantly.

q.q: Why is muddy water a suspension but milk a colloid?
q.answer: particle size|settles vs stays|filter vs not
q.explanation: Mud particles >1000 nm settle and filter out; milk fat globules 1–1000 nm stay dispersed and only show Tyndall.

q.q: Pick the correct solvation sequence for NaCl in water:
options: Hydration shells form → water faces ions → ions leave lattice
Water's δ charges face surface ions → ion-dipole attraction weakens lattice → ions leave, get hydrated → crystal shrinks
Ions evaporate → water grabs → shells break
q.explanation: Attack surface → pry loose → cage → spread — the particle mechanism.

q.q: Molarity of 0.2 mol NaOH in 500 mL solution? (M)
How many moles in 250 mL of 0.5 M KCl?
5% w/v means:
q.explanation: w/v % = grams per 100 mL of solution.

q.q: Grams of NaCl (Mᵣ 58.5) to make 200 mL of 0.5 M? (g)
Diluting 100 mL of 2.0 M to 0.5 M — final volume (mL)?
q.explanation: M₁V₁=M₂V₂ → V₂ = 2×100/0.5 = 400 mL.

q.q: The correct dilution safety rule is:
q.explanation: The big water volume absorbs the heat safely.

q.q: Molarity units are ____ per litre.
q.answer: mol|mole|moles
q.explanation: mol/L = M.

q.q: Volume of 0.25 M HCl containing 0.05 mol? (mL)
Why is molarity more useful than g/L for reaction calculations?
q.answer: counts particles|moles react 1:1|mass ignores Mr
q.explanation: Reactions combine PARTICLES (moles), not grams — molarity gives particle counts directly.

q.q: Dissolving 58.5 g NaCl in 1 L of water gives exactly 1 M solution.
q.explanation: Final volume exceeds 1 L — molarity needs solute made up TO 1 L of SOLUTION.

q.q: 20 mL of 0.1 M HCl neutralises 25 mL of NaOH. NaOH molarity? (M, 1:1)
The equivalence point is where:
options: Moles react in exact equation ratio
q.explanation: Stoichiometric truth; the colour change (end point) approximates it.

q.q: Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl. 25 mL of 0.1 M Na₂CO₃ needs how many mol of HCl?
q.explanation: n(carbonate) = 0.0025 → ×2 = 0.005 mol HCl.

q.q: Which titres should be averaged?
q.explanation: The rough run only brackets the end point.

q.q: The glassware that delivers variable measured volumes to 0.05 mL is the ____.
q.answer: burette
q.explanation: Burette for titrant; pipette for the fixed aliquot.

q.q: AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl + NaNO₃. 0.02 mol AgNO₃ + 0.03 mol NaCl → grams AgCl? (Mᵣ 143.5)
q.explanation: AgNO₃ limiting → 0.02 mol AgCl × 143.5 = 2.87 g.

q.q: Why can't you use M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ for H₂SO₄ vs NaOH?
q.answer: 1:2 ratio|two H per molecule|shortcut assumes 1:1
q.explanation: Each H₂SO₄ gives 2 H⁺ — n(NaOH) = 2×n(H₂SO₄); the 1:1 shortcut underestimates acid strength by half.

q.q: Extra distilled water in the conical flask changes the titration result.
q.explanation: Moles of analyte are fixed by the pipette — dilution in the flask doesn't alter them.

q.q: What volume of 0.2 M KOH neutralises 30 mL of 0.1 M HNO₃? (mL)
Which oxide is acidic?
q.explanation: Non-metal oxide → acid in water (sulfurous acid).

q.q: Blue litmus turns red in:
q.explanation: Acids turn blue litmus red.

q.q: The gas released when a metal reacts with acid is ____.
q.answer: hydrogen|h2
q.explanation: Metal + acid → salt + hydrogen (pop test).

q.q: Explain the difference between 'strong acid' and 'concentrated acid'.
q.answer: strong=fully ionised|concentrated=lots per volume|independent axes
q.explanation: Strong = fraction ionised (HCl 100%); concentrated = amount per volume — dilute HCl is strong but weakly concentrated.

q.q: pH 3 compared to pH 4 means the solution is:
q.explanation: Log scale: one unit = tenfold H⁺.

q.q: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Moles of NaOH to neutralise 0.05 mol H₂SO₄?
All metal oxides dissolve in water to form alkalis.
q.explanation: Only GROUP 1 + some (Ca, Ba) oxides dissolve; CuO, Fe₂O₃ are insoluble basic oxides.

q.q: Oxides like Al₂O₃ that react with both acids and bases are called ____.
q.answer: amphoteric
q.explanation: Amphoteric — dual personality.

q.q: Why does natural rainwater have pH ~5.6 even without pollution?
q.answer: CO2 carbonic acid|dissolved oxide|weak acid
q.explanation: Atmospheric CO₂ dissolves → H₂CO₃ weak acid — acidity below 5.6 signals pollution (SO₂/NO₂).

q.q: Pick the correct neutralisation products:
q.explanation: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O; the cation+anion pair is the salt.

q.q: The cation in a salt comes from the:
q.explanation: Base supplies the metal/NH₄⁺; acid supplies the anion.

q.q: Best method to prepare insoluble BaSO₄:
q.explanation: Mix soluble Ba²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ sources — filter the ppt.

q.q: The anion name from sulfuric acid is ____.
q.answer: sulfate|sulphate
q.explanation: -ic acid → -ate salt.

q.q: Why must a precipitated salt be washed before drying?
q.answer: remove adsorbed ions|spectators contaminate|purity
q.explanation: The filtrate's spectator ions coat the crystals — washing with distilled water removes them.

q.q: White curdy precipitate with AgNO₃ (acidified) identifies:
q.explanation: AgCl — the chloride signature.

q.q: The gas that turns limewater milky is ____.
q.answer: carbon dioxide|co2
q.explanation: CO₂ → CaCO₃ suspension = milkiness.

q.q: A solution of sodium carbonate is neutral (pH 7).
q.explanation: Strong base + weak acid → CO₃²⁻ hydrolyses water → alkaline (~pH 11).

q.q: Describe the test that proves a fertiliser sample contains ammonium ions.
q.answer: naoh warm|pungent gas|red litmus blue
q.explanation: NaOH + heat → NH₃ gas: pungent odour, turns damp red litmus blue.

q.q: 2HCl + CaCO₃ → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. Grams CaCl₂ from 0.05 mol HCl? (Mᵣ 111)
Pick the correct excess-solid method order:
options: Crystallise → filter → add CuO → warm acid
Warm acid → add excess CuO → filter unreacted solid → crystallise filtrate
q.explanation: Excess solid guarantees all acid used; filtration removes it; crystals from the filtrate.

q.q: Which is endothermic?
q.explanation: Plants absorb light energy to build glucose.

q.q: q (J) to warm 0.2 kg water by 5 °C? (c = 4200)
In an exothermic diagram, products are ____ reactants.
q.explanation: Energy released = products sit lower.

q.q: The minimum energy needed to start a reaction is ____ energy.
q.answer: activation|ea
q.explanation: The hump on every energy diagram.

q.q: Is bond breaking exothermic or endothermic? Explain why making bonds is the opposite.
q.answer: breaking costs|making releases|energy payback
q.explanation: Separating bonded atoms requires energy input; forming bonds releases that energy as the pair falls to lower energy.

q.q: Broken = 2644 kJ, made = 3338 kJ. ΔH (kJ/mol)?
Exothermic reactions release more energy making bonds than they consume breaking them.
q.explanation: That net payback IS the released heat.

q.q: 100 mL solution rose 6.8 °C (c = 4200, ρ = 1 g/mL). q in J?
Why does condensation form UNDER a cold-pack beaker?
q.answer: cools air below dew point|water vapour condenses|surroundings lost heat
q.explanation: The endothermic dissolution cools the glass, which cools the air touching it — its water vapour condenses.

q.q: Pick the correct calorimetry chain:
q.explanation: Measure temperature, compute heat, divide by moles, apply sign.

q.q: In a galvanic cell, oxidation occurs at the:
q.explanation: Anode = oxidation, always (OIL RIG anchor).

q.q: Which pair gives the highest voltage?
q.explanation: Mg-Cu has the biggest reactivity gap (~1.6 V).

q.q: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss of ____.
q.answer: electrons|electron
q.explanation: Loss of electrons = oxidation.

q.q: Why can't you get sodium metal by electrolyising aqueous NaCl?
q.answer: h+ discharges first|water competes|only molten works
q.explanation: H⁺ from water is easier to reduce than Na⁺ — you get H₂ gas; sodium needs MOLTEN NaCl with no water present.

q.q: In electroplating silver, the object being plated is the:
q.explanation: Cathode attracts Ag⁺ which reduces onto it.

q.q: Pick the correct electron path in a Zn-Cu cell:
options: Zn → wire → Cu; ions in solution
q.explanation: Electrons: anode (Zn) through wire to cathode (Cu); ions handle the solution leg.

q.q: Cells connected in series add their voltages.
q.explanation: 3 × 1.5 V = 4.5 V — that's how torch batteries stack.

q.q: The mineral additive that lets alumina melt at ~950 °C is ____.
q.answer: cryolite
q.explanation: Cryolite (Na₃AlF₆) — the aluminium industry's energy saver.

q.q: A torch needs 4.5 V from 1.5 V cells in series. How many cells?
At a carbon anode in the aluminium cell, why must the anode be replaced regularly?
q.answer: oxygen burns carbon|co2 forms|anode corrodes
q.explanation: O²⁻ discharges to O₂ which reacts with the carbon anode → CO₂ — the electrode is consumed by its own product.

q.q: Metals conduct electricity because of:
q.explanation: Mobile delocalised electrons drift under a potential difference.

q.q: Which metal is extracted by electrolysis rather than carbon reduction?
q.explanation: Al is too reactive — carbon cannot reduce Al₂O₃; electricity supplies the electrons.

q.q: Mass of Fe (g) from full reduction of 160 g Fe₂O₃? (Fe₂O₃=160, Fe=56)
q.explanation: 1 mol Fe₂O₃ → 2 mol Fe = 112 g.

q.q: The actual reducing agent inside a blast furnace is carbon ____.
q.answer: monoxide|co
q.explanation: CO₂ + C → 2CO; CO then reduces the iron oxide.

q.q: Why is limestone added to the blast furnace?
q.answer: removes impurities slag|forms calcium silicate|removes sand silica
q.explanation: CaCO₃ → CaO; CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃ slag, which floats and is tapped off.

q.q: Cryolite in aluminium electrolysis serves to:
q.explanation: It dissolves Al₂O₃ so electrolysis runs at ~950 °C instead of ~2050 °C.

q.q: Mercury is a liquid metal at room temperature.
q.explanation: The classic exception — Hg melts at −39 °C.

q.q: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂. Moles of H₂ from 0.5 mol Zn (excess acid)?
q.explanation: 1:1 ratio → 0.5 mol H₂.

q.q: How does galvanising protect scratched steel?
q.answer: sacrificial zinc|zinc corrodes instead|zinc more reactive
q.explanation: Zn is above Fe in the series — it oxidises preferentially, feeding electrons to the iron even at a scratch.

q.q: Pick the correct reaction sequence for CO formation in the blast furnace:
options: CO₂ + C → 2CO then C + O₂ → CO₂
C + O₂ → CO₂ then CO₂ + C → 2CO
Fe₂O₃ + CO → Fe then C + O₂ → CO
CaCO₃ → CaO then C + O₂ → CO₂
q.explanation: Coke burns first (heat), then hot coke reduces the CO₂ up the stack to CO — the ore reducer.

q.q: A glowing splint RELIGHTS in a jar. The gas is:
q.explanation: Oxygen supports combustion — the classic relight test.

q.q: The catalyst used in H₂O₂ lab oxygen preparation is ____ dioxide.
q.answer: manganese|mno2
q.explanation: MnO₂ speeds decomposition and is unchanged.

q.q: Industrial hydrogen is mainly made by:
q.explanation: CH₄ + H₂O(g) → CO + 3H₂ (Ni catalyst) — cheap bulk route.

q.q: Haber: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. Moles of NH₃ from 2 mol N₂ (excess H₂)?
q.explanation: 1:2 ratio → 4 mol NH₃.

q.q: Why does the Haber process use high PRESSURE?
q.answer: fewer moles right|shifts equilibrium to ammonia|4 mol gas become 2
q.explanation: Left has 4 gas moles, right 2 — pressure favours the side with fewer molecules (more NH₃).

q.q: Chlorine is produced industrially by:
q.explanation: Chlor-alkali electrolysis: Cl⁻ oxidised at the anode.

q.q: Damp blue litmus bleached white indicates chlorine gas.
q.explanation: Cl₂ + water makes HClO — a strong oxidising bleach.

q.q: The catalyst in the contact process (SO₂ → SO₃) is vanadium(__) oxide.
q.answer: five|v2o5|5
q.explanation: V₂O₅ at ~450 °C.

q.q: Mass of H₂SO₄ (g) from 32 g sulfur (1:1 chain)? (S=32, H₂SO₄=98)
q.explanation: 1 mol S → 1 mol H₂SO₄ = 98 g.

q.q: Choose the correct contact-process order:
q.explanation: Burn sulfur, catalyse to SO₃, absorb in acid (oleum), then dilute.

q.q: The general formula of alkenes is:
q.explanation: One double bond removes 2 H from the alkane formula.

q.q: How many hydrogens in the alkane with 8 carbons (octane, CₙH₂ₙ₊₂)?
Bromine water shaken with an unknown hydrocarbon turns colourless. The hydrocarbon is:
q.explanation: Addition across C=C consumes Br₂ — the unsaturation test.

q.q: Name the reaction type: CH₄ + Cl₂ →(UV) CH₃Cl + HCl.
q.answer: substitution
q.explanation: Chlorine substitutes a hydrogen; UV light drives the radical chain.

q.q: Balance C₃H₈ + _O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. Coefficient of O₂?
q.explanation: O right: 6+4 = 10 → 5 O₂.

q.q: How many structural isomers does C₅H₁₂ have?
q.explanation: Pentane, 2-methylbutane, 2,2-dimethylpropane.

q.q: Why is cracking important to a refinery?
q.answer: heavy fractions to petrol|makes alkenes too|demand for short chains
q.explanation: Crude yields too much heavy wax vs petrol demand; cracking converts heavy → light alkane (fuel) + alkene (plastics feedstock).

q.q: Ethyne (acetylene) is used in oxy-acetylene welding because its flame reaches very high temperature.
q.explanation: C₂H₂ + O₂ burns at ~3200 °C — hot enough to cut and weld steel.

q.q: Pick the correct polymerisation equation for ethene:
q.explanation: Addition polymerisation: double bonds open and link into the polyethene chain.

q.q: The test that distinguishes saturated from unsaturated hydrocarbons uses ____ water.
q.answer: bromine
q.explanation: Bromine water: orange → colourless means unsaturated.

q.q: Benzene's bonding is best described as:
options: A ring with delocalised π electrons
q.explanation: All six p-electrons spread over the ring — equal bonds, extra stability.

q.q: Benzene reacts with bromine:
options: Only by substitution with FeBr₃ catalyst
q.explanation: Addition would break aromatic stability; catalysed substitution keeps the ring.

q.q: The reagent pair for nitrating benzene is nitric acid plus concentrated ____ acid.
q.answer: sulfur|sulphuric|h2so4
q.explanation: Conc H₂SO₄ catalyses (generates the nitronium ion).

q.q: Balance 2C₆H₆ + _O₂ → 12CO₂ + 6H₂O. Coefficient of O₂?
q.explanation: O right: 24 + 6 = 30 → 15 O₂.

q.q: Which fraction of crude oil distillation exits at the TOP of the column?
q.explanation: Lowest boiling → stays vapour to the cold top.

q.q: Phenol (C₆H₅OH) is classified as an alcohol.
q.explanation: OH on a benzene ring = phenol — a weak acid with distinct chemistry, not an alcohol.

q.q: Why does benzene NOT decolourise bromine water despite being 'unsaturated'?
q.answer: delocalisation too stable|addition destroys ring stability|aromatic stability
q.explanation: Addition would sacrifice ~152 kJ/mol of delocalisation energy — thermodynamics says no.

q.q: Natural gas from Ethiopia's Calub field is mostly:
q.explanation: Natural gas ≈ methane; it feeds national power plants.

q.q: Reduction of nitrobenzene yields ____ (aromatic amine).
q.answer: aniline|c6h5nh2|aminobenzene
q.explanation: C₆H₅NO₂ + 6[H] → C₆H₅NH₂ + 2H₂O — the dye/drug gateway.

q.q: Choose the correct coalification sequence:
q.explanation: Increasing pressure/time raises carbon content: peat → lignite → bituminous → anthracite.

q.q: The word democracy was derived from two Greek words meaning:
q.explanation: Demos means the people and kratos means rule.

q.q: Which statement best reflects the textbook position on defining democracy?
options: The term is elastic and changes with time, place and circumstance
q.explanation: The textbook says there is no absolute definition and the term is elastic.

q.q: There is no absolute definition of democracy.
q.explanation: The lesson states clearly that there is no absolute definition.

q.q: The dictionary definition says that people hold ruling power:
options: either directly or indirectly through elected representatives
q.explanation: People hold the ruling power either directly or indirectly through elected representatives.

q.q: Name the two Greek words from which democracy is derived.
q.answer: demos and kratos|demo and kratos
q.explanation: Democracy comes from demos (people) and kratos (rule).

q.q: Give the term for the complex, long-term, dynamic and open-ended process of moving a political system into democracy.
q.answer: democratization
q.explanation: This is the definition of democratization.

q.q: Which of the following is an example of democratization?
options: A transition from authoritarian rule to a full democracy
q.explanation: Democratization is a transition towards a more democratic regime.

q.q: A transition from a semi-authoritarian political system to a democratic political system is a form of democratization.
q.explanation: The lesson lists this as one of the transitions that count as democratization.

q.q: Explain in one sentence why state power in a democracy involves compromise and bargaining.
q.answer: different interests must be balanced|decisions need agreement among differing views
q.explanation: Many groups hold different interests, so democratic decisions require give and take.

q.q: Arrange these regimes from least democratic to most democratic.
q.explanation: The order runs from authoritarian regime through semi-authoritarian system and semi-democracy to full democracy.

q.q: Democratization is best described as:
options: the transition to a more democratic system of government
q.explanation: Democratization is the transition to a more democratic system of government.

q.q: Political parties are described in the lesson as:
q.explanation: The textbook calls political parties vectors of democracy.

q.q: Political parties are essential to the functioning and durability of democracy.
q.explanation: The lesson states that parties are essential to the functioning and durability of democracy.

q.q: The main difference between political parties and civil society organizations is that:
options: civil society cannot exist in a democracy
they differ in their final goal
civil society seeks to win elections
q.explanation: Like parties they are vectors of democracy, but they differ from parties in their final goal.

q.q: Give the other name used in the lesson for an interest group.
q.answer: pressure group
q.explanation: A pressure group is also called an interest group.

q.q: Interest groups are called transmission belts because they:
options: bridge the gap between citizens and government
q.explanation: Interest groups bridge the gap between the citizen and government.

q.q: Give the name of the third sector of society that is distinct from government and business.
q.answer: civil society
q.explanation: Civil society is understood as the third sector of society.

q.q: The importance of the mass media in a country depends on:
options: the number of private radio stations
the quality of the information provided to the public
q.explanation: The textbook says importance depends on the quality of information, not on the number of outlets.

q.q: The media can build democratic culture only when it is free, independent and well resourced.
q.explanation: To perform its functions the media must be free, independent and sufficiently resourced.

q.q: Which of the following is an interest group rather than a political party?
options: A party that contests national elections
A traders' association that lobbies for lower tariffs
q.explanation: An association that seeks to influence policy without seeking to govern is an interest group.

q.q: Explain in one sentence why the efficiency of civil society depends on its autonomy.
q.answer: dependent groups cannot freely defend rights|autonomy lets them act independently of government
q.explanation: The efficiency of civil society depends on the extent to which associations are autonomous or institutionalized.

q.q: Arrange the steps by which an interest group influences policy.
options: Members with a shared concern organize
q.explanation: The order is: members organize, state demands, contact officials, then keep watch over the policy.

q.q: Democratic institutions are important because they:
q.explanation: Democratic institutions are the institutions that make democracy work.

q.q: Autocratic and oligarchic governments might have the rule of law but do not qualify as democracies.
q.explanation: They fail to fully ensure equality under the law.

q.q: Which of the following is NOT a function of the independent national electoral commission?
q.explanation: Foreign policy is a government function, not a function of the electoral commission.

q.q: Name the body charged with organizing, conducting and supervising elections in a country.
q.answer: independent national electoral commission|INEC
q.explanation: This is the independent national electoral commission.

q.q: Which body registers political parties and monitors their campaigns?
q.explanation: Registering parties and monitoring their organization and campaigns is a function of the electoral commission.

q.q: Give the other name for a pressure group.
q.answer: interest group
q.explanation: A pressure group is also called an interest group.

q.q: A pressure group that examines public policies and reports on them is acting as:
q.explanation: Acting as a watchdog over public policies is a listed function of pressure groups.

q.q: Strong democratic institutions are difficult to manipulate and enable the honest to survive.
q.explanation: The lesson says strong institutions are respected, hard to manipulate and enable the honest to survive.

q.q: Which statement best explains why a one-party system is not a principle of a democratic system?
options: It reduces political competition and accountability
q.explanation: Democracy requires competition and accountability, which a one-party system removes.

q.q: Explain in one sentence why equality under the law is the test that separates democratic from autocratic institutions.
q.answer: autocracies may follow law but deny equality|democracy requires serving all equally
q.explanation: Autocratic and oligarchic governments may have the rule of law but fail to ensure equality for all.

q.q: Arrange these electoral tasks in the correct order.
q.explanation: The electorate is educated first, then the date is fixed, then officers and materials are provided, and finally the election is conducted.

q.q: Social transformation is the process by which an individual alters:
options: the socially ascribed status of his or her parents into an achieved status
q.explanation: This is the definition of status transformation given in the lesson.

q.q: The individual sense of social transformation applies to a person, while the societal sense applies to the social system.
q.explanation: The first applies to an individual and the second to the social system.

q.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the ways the lesson says transformation is manifested?
q.explanation: The listed ways are social change, civic engagement, civic dialogue, social capital and community development.

q.q: Give the term for the collective value of all social networks and the inclination to do things for each other.
q.answer: social capital
q.explanation: This is the definition of social capital.

q.q: The defining characteristic of active civic engagement is:
options: commitment to participate in and contribute to the improvement of one's community and nation
q.explanation: Civic engagement is defined by commitment to participate and contribute to improvement.

q.q: Give the term for dialogue in which people explore matters of civic importance and differing viewpoints work toward common understanding.
q.answer: civic dialogue
q.explanation: This is the definition of civic dialogue.

q.q: In civic dialogue, participants are encouraged to:
options: promote a single point of view
suspend judgment and bring assumptions into the open
win the argument at any cost
q.explanation: Suspension of judgment and bringing assumptions into the open are encouraged in civic dialogue.

q.q: Social change must start with the individual.
q.explanation: The lesson states that acknowledging this, social change must start with the individual.

q.q: Bonding networks connect people who are similar and sustain:
q.explanation: Bonding networks sustain particularized in-group reciprocity.

q.q: Explain in one sentence how social capital helps a community finish a shared project.
q.answer: trust and reciprocity make cooperation easier|networks reduce the cost of working together
q.explanation: Networks produce trust, reciprocity, information and cooperation, which make joint work easier.

q.q: Name one focus of community development agencies mentioned in the lesson.
q.answer: job training|workforce development|housing|small business start-up|youth development|health|recreation
q.explanation: Agencies focus on housing, job training, commercial development, small business start-up and other community goals.

q.q: The three core values central to democracy are:
q.explanation: The three core values are liberty or freedom, justice and equality.

q.q: Personal freedom means individuals should be free from arbitrary arrest and detention.
q.explanation: Personal freedom includes freedom from arbitrary arrest and detention.

q.q: Which of the following is an example of electoral corruption that violates political freedom?
q.explanation: Buying votes is listed as electoral corruption against political freedom.

q.q: Distributive justice is about:
options: distributing benefits and burdens in society by agreed standards of fairness
q.explanation: Distributive justice distributes benefits and burdens by agreed standards of fairness.

q.q: Give the sense of justice that requires impartial and open procedures for gathering information and making decisions.
q.answer: procedural justice
q.explanation: This is procedural justice.

q.q: Give the notion of equality that means one person, one vote, one value.
q.answer: political equality
q.explanation: Political equality means equal political rights, one person, one vote, one value.

q.q: Economic freedom in the lesson includes the right to:
options: acquire, use, transfer and dispose of private property
q.explanation: Economic freedom covers acquiring, using, transferring and disposing of private property.

q.q: Explain in one sentence why buying votes damages both political freedom and equality.
q.answer: money replaces free choice and makes votes unequal|it corrupts free participation and the equal value of votes
q.explanation: Vote buying is electoral corruption and it destroys the equal value of each vote.

q.q: Social equality implies that:
options: there should be no social hierarchy and no discrimination whatsoever
q.explanation: Social equality means no social hierarchy and no discrimination at individual or collective level.

q.q: Corrective justice means that a proportional response should be in place to correct wrongs and injuries.
q.explanation: This is the textbook definition of corrective justice.

q.q: A court returns a stolen bicycle to its owner and fines the thief. This best illustrates:
q.explanation: A proportional response to a wrong is corrective justice.

q.q: The three aspects of democracy are:
q.explanation: Democracy has social, economic and political aspects.

q.q: The social aspect of democracy requires the removal of discrimination based on class, caste, creed, colour, sex, ethnicity or race.
q.explanation: This is exactly what the social aspect requires.

q.q: The economic aspect of democracy requires:
options: equitable and just distribution of wealth and resources
removal of the right to work
q.explanation: The economic aspect means equitable and just distribution of wealth and resources.

q.q: Which aspect of democracy provides the right to vote and the right to contest elections?
q.answer: political aspect|the political aspect of democracy
q.explanation: Political rights belong to the political aspect of democracy.

q.q: The right to work, leisure, fair wages and enjoyment of life belongs to:
q.explanation: Economic democracy recognizes these rights.

q.q: Give the term used in the lesson to describe democracy as a balance of interests among social groups.
q.answer: social balance
q.explanation: Democracy is described as a social balance.

q.q: Which freedoms must citizens have in order to exercise political rights effectively?
options: freedom of speech, association and publication
q.explanation: Citizens have to be assured freedom of speech, association and publication.

q.q: A country with free elections but severe social discrimination is only partly democratic.
q.explanation: The social aspect of democracy requires the removal of discrimination.

q.q: Which situation best shows the absence of the economic aspect of democracy?
options: A small group owns most wealth while many workers earn below a living wage
q.explanation: Glaring disparities and polarization based on wealth contradict the economic aspect.

q.q: Explain in one sentence why political rights without freedom of speech are ineffective.
q.answer: citizens cannot use or defend their rights without speaking|rights on paper need free speech to be used
q.explanation: Citizens must have freedom of speech, association and publication to use their political rights.

q.q: Name one form of discrimination that the social aspect of democracy removes.
q.answer: class|caste|creed|colour|sex|ethnicity|race
q.explanation: The social aspect removes discrimination based on class, caste, creed, colour, sex, ethnicity or race.

q.q: According to the lesson, digital technology has which impact on citizens?
q.explanation: Digital technology creates positive and negative impacts on citizens' emotions, social life and ethical values.

q.q: Moderate use of digital technology produces positive effects on citizens.
q.explanation: Moderate use produces positive effects, while excessive and addictive use produces negative effects.

q.q: People with higher social media use are more likely to:
q.explanation: People with higher social media use are more likely to feel socially isolated than those who do not use it often.

q.q: What is the change of human identity from real life to artificial or imaginary life called?
q.answer: secondhand living
q.explanation: This is secondhand living, where life is experienced through digital media rather than firsthand.

q.q: Briefly explain what internet addiction means.
q.answer: compulsive overuse of social media games or messaging|wasting time and money for low return
q.explanation: Social media, games, messaging and dating sites can be addictive, and users waste vast time and money for low return.

q.q: Kobalo had many friends but became addicted to online gaming and isolated himself. This is an example of:
q.explanation: Overuse and addiction led to social alienation, a negative social effect.

q.q: Digital technology has the power to change the nature of human interactions.
q.explanation: The textbook states that digital technology can change the nature of human interactions.

q.q: Name one negative effect of digital technology on citizens' ethical values.
q.answer: untruthfulness|ethical dilemma|creating unhappiness|increasing uncertainty|fake news
q.explanation: Negative ethical effects include ethical dilemma, uncertainty, unhappiness, untruthfulness and eroded freedom.

q.q: Which of the following is a positive effect of digital technology on emotions?
q.explanation: Mobile phones give people a sense of security in public spaces, while the others are negative effects.

q.q: Arrange the chain that leads from moderate use to social alienation.
q.explanation: The chain begins with moderate use, then longer hours, neglect of real contact, addiction and finally isolation.

q.q: Name one use of digital technology that improves health care according to the lesson.
q.answer: online appointments|remote treatment|medical information|treatment by specialists
q.explanation: Digital technology gives patients quick medical information and access to specialists anywhere in the world.

q.q: The electronic standard of conduct or procedure is called:
q.explanation: Etiquette is the electronic standard of conduct or procedure.

q.q: Digital behaviour makes everyone a role model.
q.explanation: Etiquette means understanding how digital behaviour affects others, and every user is a role model.

q.q: Which action breaks the ethical code of responsibility?
options: Citing the author of a source
Copying internet material for a project without credit
q.explanation: Copying material without giving credit is an example of inappropriate responsibility.

q.q: Name the ethical code that means protecting electronic data with virus protection, firewalls and updates.
q.answer: security|digital security
q.explanation: Security means protecting electronic data and protecting people from harm.

q.q: Why is accuracy or trustworthiness important on the internet?
q.answer: no agency monitors truth|false information spreads confusion|can cause medical and legal problems
q.explanation: There is no agency monitoring the truth of information, so inaccurate information can cause confusion and medical or legal problems.

q.q: Telling a friend your email and Facebook passwords is a failure of:
q.explanation: Confidentiality protects private information such as passwords.

q.q: Carpal tunnel syndrome, eyestrain and poor posture are concerns of the ethical code of safety.
q.explanation: Safety concerns the physical dangers inherent in using technology, including these problems.

q.q: Which is an example of inappropriate etiquette in school?
options: Sending non-class related messages during class
Turning off a phone in an examination
q.explanation: Sending non-class related messages during class is an example of inappropriate etiquette.

q.q: Explain why developing digital citizenship is important for young people.
q.answer: active engaged and respectful users|fosters digital skills and inclusion|protects from risks
q.explanation: Ensuring the young are active, engaged and respectful online fosters digital skill development and inclusion and reduces risk.

q.q: Give the name for the protection of computer systems and networks from information disclosure and theft.
q.answer: cyber security|cybersecurity
q.explanation: This is the definition of cyber security.

q.q: Arrange the steps of using online information responsibly.
options: Use it in your own words and cite the source
Check whether it is accurate and trustworthy
Decide whether it is ethical and legal to use
q.explanation: The order is to find, check accuracy, decide whether it is ethical and legal, then use it with credit.

q.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the opportunities of digital technology for young citizens listed in the lesson?
q.explanation: Social isolation is a negative effect, not an opportunity.

q.q: Digital technology allows lessons and courses to be delivered virtually online.
q.explanation: Learning opportunities include virtual online lessons and courses.

q.q: Remote working has become common because of:
q.explanation: Increased connectivity means many people can work from home.

q.q: What name is given to doing a job from a distance using digital technology instead of being at the workplace?
q.answer: remote working|working from home
q.explanation: This is remote working.

q.q: Explain how digital technology provides learning opportunities for the young.
q.answer: online lessons and courses|access to world knowledge|learn directly from sources|short-term trainings
q.explanation: The internet gives access to the world's knowledge, virtual courses, direct learning and short-term trainings.

q.q: A young person uses online tutorials, forums and a phone to build a new app. This best shows:
q.explanation: Information access, connectivity and digital learning enable creativity and innovation.

q.q: Digital technology enables young citizens to take short-term trainings in different disciplines.
q.explanation: The lesson states that digital technology enables the young to acquire short-term trainings.

q.q: Why does information access make a young citizen better informed?
q.answer: knows local and world events|open access to information|can join collaborative activities
